strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: directly processing NeRF weights across heterogeneous architectures, rather than requiring a fixed parameterization or rendering views first.

The use of a Graph Meta-Network is technically well motivated, and pairing it with a contrastive objective is a simple, coherent way to align representations of the same object encoded by different NeRF architectures.
The experiments use a reasonably large paired dataset and examine classification, class-level retrieval, instance-level retrieval, and transfer to several architectural variants.

The loss ablations are informative: the results consistently show the trade-off between the class separability induced by the rendering loss and the cross-architecture invariance induced by the contrastive loss.

Results on seen architectures are strong, and the single-architecture model slightly improves over nf2vec and Cardace et al. The appendix also provides useful architecture, optimization, dataset, runtime, and hardware details.
weaknesses: The central claims of handling “arbitrary” or “any” NeRF architecture are substantially stronger than the evidence. Training covers only an MLP and one tri-plane design, while the nominally unseen architectures merely change layer count, hidden width, grid resolution, or channel count within those same two families. No genuinely different representation, such as a hash grid, voxel grid, tensor factorization, or view-dependent NeRF, is tested.

Generalization is fragile for some architectural changes. For example, accuracy on TRI-8C is only 11.4–21.3% for the contrastive variants, and TRI-16W can fall to 30.1% for the rendering-loss model. These failures conflict with the broad robustness claims and are not analyzed sufficiently.

The multi-architecture setting lacks competitive baselines. Declaring prior methods inapplicable is not enough: reasonable alternatives include separate architecture-specific encoders with a shared or aligned latent space, distillation-based alignment, pooled render/image features, and simple ensembles or late-fusion systems. Consequently, the main proposed setting is evaluated almost entirely through comparisons among the authors’ own loss variants.

Novelty is moderate. The principal method is an application of an existing parameter-graph GMN and an existing nf2vec decoder, augmented with a standard SigLIP objective on naturally paired examples. The paper does not introduce a new architectural mechanism or theoretical result explaining cross-architecture generalization.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic, object-centric ShapeNetRender data with 13 classes. There is no evidence on real scenes, larger or more modern NeRFs, view-dependent appearance, noisy training, or NeRFs produced by different optimization pipelines and random seeds.

Results are reported as single numbers without repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance testing. This is especially problematic for the small single-architecture improvements over prior work.

The practical motivation emphasizes avoiding rendering cost, but the paper does not report inference time, graph-construction overhead, memory consumption, parameter count, or comparisons with render-based alternatives. Training takes roughly two weeks per rendering-based model on an RTX 3090, raising efficiency concerns.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: no code or trained-model release is stated, and important graph-construction and feature details are largely delegated to prior work. Hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly for the contrastive weight, is also absent.

The paper does not report decoder rendering fidelity or other direct measures of information preservation, making it difficult to determine whether the learned representation captures radiance-field content beyond the selected classification and retrieval tasks.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of weight-space NeRF processing: existing methods are tied to fixed parameterizations, whereas graph meta-networks can in principle accept variable computational structures.
Combining a graph meta-network with rendering and cross-architecture contrastive objectives is conceptually coherent, and the paper clearly explains the intended roles of the two losses.

The experiments include classification, instance- and class-level retrieval, loss ablations, and tests involving several held-out width/depth/resolution variants. Cross-architecture retrieval shows a substantial benefit from contrastive training.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and provides useful implementation and training details.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling “arbitrary” NeRF architectures is substantially overstated. Training covers only an MLP and a tri-plane-plus-MLP, while the purported unseen architectures merely change widths, depths, channel counts, or grid resolution. No genuinely new architectural family—such as hash grids, voxel grids, or modern real-scene NeRFs—is tested.

Generalization is inconsistent and sometimes collapses under modest architectural changes. For example, the contrastive variants obtain only 11–21% accuracy on TRI-8C in the multi-architecture setting, and single-architecture transfer often approaches chance. These results do not convincingly support robust architecture-agnostic inference.

The evaluation lacks essential architecture-agnostic baselines. Rendering views followed by established image/3D encoders, sampling each NeRF as a canonical function, or using separate architecture-specific encoders with embedding alignment would provide meaningful comparisons. Declaring nf2vec and Cardace et al. inapplicable leaves most central tables without competing methods.

The method requires paired NeRFs of exactly the same objects instantiated in both training architectures. Producing such paired representations is expensive and unusually strong supervision; the study does not establish whether the claimed invariance transfers beyond the two paired architecture families or works with unpaired collections.

Technical novelty is limited: the approach largely combines an existing graph meta-network, the existing nf2vec decoder/rendering objective, and the existing SigLIP loss. The paper offers little new architectural or theoretical insight beyond applying these components to paired NeRFs.

The combined objective does not deliver a consistently strong universal representation: rendering-only training is best for standard classification, contrastive-only training is best for instance retrieval, and the combined loss often trails the task-specific choice. Even its t-SNE visualization retains architecture-specific subclusters, contradicting the strongest invariance language.

All results use one synthetic ShapeNetRender collection with the same 13 classes and two legacy NeRF parameterizations. There is no evaluation on real scenes, different datasets, downstream geometric tasks, or contemporary NeRF architectures, severely limiting practical significance.

No results across random seeds, uncertainty estimates, statistical tests, or systematic sensitivity analysis for the loss weight are reported. Given several small claimed improvements over prior work, it is unclear whether those gains are reliable.

Efficiency is insufficiently evaluated despite efficiency motivating direct weight processing. Training takes roughly two weeks per rendering-based model on an RTX 3090, yet the paper reports no inference time, graph-construction cost, peak memory, parameter count, or comparison against render-and-encode alternatives.

Reproducibility is only partial: architecture and optimizer details are given, but no code or trained-model release is stated, and the expensive training procedure plus newly generated held-out NeRF sets makes independent replication difficult.

strengths: Addresses a timely and meaningful limitation of prior weight-space NeRF methods: dependence on a fixed input architecture.
The graph meta-network formulation is technically well motivated and naturally accommodates variable parameter-graph structures.
Combining rendering and contrastive objectives is sensible, and the ablations clearly reveal their complementary effects on class separability and architecture invariance.
The evaluation covers classification, class-level retrieval, instance-level retrieval, cross-architecture transfer, and several architectures unseen during training.

Results are generally strong: the method matches or exceeds architecture-specific baselines in the single-architecture setting and enables multi-architecture tasks those baselines cannot directly support.
The paper is clearly organized, relates the method well to prior work, and provides useful architectural, optimization, dataset, and hardware details.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling arbitrary NeRF architectures is substantially broader than the evidence. Training covers only MLP and tri-plane families, while unseen architectures are nearby depth, width, resolution, or channel-count variants rather than genuinely new families such as hash grids, voxel grids, or tensor decompositions.
All experiments use one synthetic, object-centric ShapeNetRender benchmark. Generalization to real images, complex scenes, varying appearance conditions, or other datasets is untested.

There is no competitive baseline in the main multi-architecture setting. Although existing published methods cannot directly operate there, reasonable alternatives such as aligned architecture-specific encoders or simpler parameter-graph baselines would better isolate the value of the GMN.

Generalization to unseen variants is uneven and sometimes very poor—for example, accuracy on TRI-8C falls to roughly 11–21% for the contrastive variants—so the architecture-agnostic characterization needs qualification.

The contrastive approach requires paired NeRFs of the same object under different architectures during training, which may be expensive or unavailable in practical collections and is not sufficiently discussed as a limitation.
Results lack multiple-seed statistics, confidence intervals, and sensitivity studies for the loss weight and other important choices, making it difficult to assess robustness.

The method is computationally heavy—approximately two weeks of training on an RTX 3090 for rendering-based variants—yet runtime, memory scaling with parameter-graph size, and inference cost are not analyzed.
Instance-level retrieval remains modest, with only 29% recall@1 in the broadest setting, indicating that architecture-invariant instance information is far from reliably captured.

strengths: Addresses a relevant limitation of prior weight-space NeRF methods: their dependence on a fixed architecture. Representing NeRF parameters as graphs is a sensible way to support variable topology and parameter counts.

The combination of rendering and contrastive objectives is well motivated. The experiments clearly show their complementary behavior: rendering improves class separability, while contrastive alignment substantially improves transfer and cross-architecture retrieval.

The evaluation covers 13 configurations across MLP, tri-plane, and hash-grid families. Introducing a compact parameter-graph construction for multi-resolution hash tables is a useful technical contribution.
The paper is clearly written and provides substantial implementation detail, including graph construction, model architecture, optimization settings, dataset sizes, and hardware requirements.
weaknesses: The central architecture-agnostic claim is substantially broader than the evidence. Every unseen architecture is only a hyperparameter variation within one of three training-time families; the method is not evaluated on a genuinely unseen family, computation graph, layer type, or view-dependent NeRF formulation. Moreover, each family requires a manually designed graph conversion.

The empirical scope is narrow: nearly all results use the same synthetic, object-centric ShapeNetRender split with simplified view-independent NeRFs. Cross-dataset generalization is assessed only qualitatively on a few Objaverse examples, with no quantitative evaluation on realistic objects or scenes.

The most direct evidence for architecture invariance is not especially strong. With mixed-family query and gallery sets, LR+C obtains only 5.3% Recall@1 and 27.2% Recall@10. Several unseen configurations also cause severe classification failures, such as TRI-8C and HASH-11T. Describing the overall behavior as robust therefore overstates the results.

Baseline coverage is insufficient in the main multi-architecture setting. Although prior weight encoders cannot directly process all families, the paper does not compare against practical alternatives such as rendering-based embeddings, embeddings of sampled radiance-field outputs, family-specific encoder ensembles, supervised GMN training, or simpler graph/parameter-statistics baselines. Consequently, it remains unclear whether direct weight processing provides a meaningful accuracy-efficiency advantage.

The method depends on matched NeRFs of the same object trained under multiple architectures. This is expensive supervision and a restrictive dataset construction assumption, but its necessity, scaling behavior, and performance with fewer paired architectures or objects are not studied.

Important controls are missing: there are no multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, significance tests, sensitivity analyses for the contrastive weight or batch construction, or comparisons of encoder capacity and computational cost. Since training takes roughly two weeks on an A6000, reproducibility and efficiency are material concerns.

Rendering quality for the newly trained and reduced-capacity NeRF variants is not reported. Thus, poor transfer on variants such as HASH-11T could reflect degradation of the underlying NeRF content rather than failure or success of architectural generalization.

The technical novelty is moderate: the framework largely combines an existing GMN, the nf2vec decoder, and a standard SigLIP objective. The hash-table graph is useful but relatively straightforward, while the small gains over prior methods in the single-architecture setting do not establish a large broader advance.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem: learning directly from NeRF weights when the input networks do not share one fixed architecture.
Using a Graph Meta-Network is a natural technical choice, and the proposed compact parameter-graph construction for multi-resolution hash tables is sensible.

The combination of rendering and cross-architecture contrastive objectives is intuitively motivated. The ablations show that the contrastive term substantially improves transfer between the three architecture families.

The study covers 13 configurations, and the method obtains strong classification accuracy when training and testing conditions are closely matched. The manuscript is generally clear and includes useful implementation details.
weaknesses: The central claim of architecture-agnostic representation learning is substantially stronger than the evidence. All experiments use only three closely controlled architecture families, and the supposedly unseen architectures are merely hyperparameter variations within those families. There is no evaluation on a genuinely unseen family or substantially different NeRF formulation.

Generalization is brittle even within known families. Accuracy drops dramatically for changes such as TRI-8C and HASH-11T, sometimes from roughly 90% to around 25–31%. The t-SNE plots also retain architecture-dependent substructure. These results undermine claims of robust processing of unseen architectures.

The central multi-architecture setting lacks meaningful competing baselines: prior methods are simply marked inapplicable. Comparisons to family-specific encoder ensembles, render-based representations, supervised GMNs, generic network-representation methods, or simple parameter-statistics baselines would be needed to establish the value of the proposed formulation.

Instance retrieval performance is weak in absolute terms. On ALL/ALL, recall@1 is only 5.3% and recall@10 is 27.2%. No random-chance, render-based, or other retrieval baseline is reported, while qualitative examples cannot establish competitive retrieval quality and may be selectively favorable.

The method called unsupervised requires explicit instance correspondences: every object must be trained as multiple NeRF architectures so those representations can form positive pairs. This is consequential supervision and a costly assumption that is unlikely to hold for naturally collected NeRF repositories. The paper does not test robustness to missing, noisy, or sparse correspondences.

The evaluation is almost entirely restricted to synthetic ShapeNetRender objects. Cross-dataset generalization is assessed only through a few qualitative Objaverse queries using an already-seen MLP architecture, without quantitative results. This is insufficient to support broad applicability to real NeRF collections.

Experimental rigor is limited: results have no multiple-seed averages, error bars, or significance analysis, despite some claimed improvements over prior single-architecture methods being only 0.9–1.5 percentage points.

Important ablations and efficiency measurements are absent, including sensitivity to the contrastive-loss weight, alternative pooling or graph constructions, representation dimensionality, scaling with network size, inference memory and runtime, and the contribution of individual graph metadata fields. This is especially problematic because training takes approximately two weeks on an A6000 and efficiency motivates processing weights directly.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper does not provide sufficiently detailed NeRF-training and dataset-generation specifications or a clear code/data release commitment, particularly for the newly generated hash-based and unseen-architecture datasets.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of prior weight-space NeRF methods: their dependence on a fixed input architecture. Representing NeRF parameters as graphs and using a Graph Meta-Network is a well-motivated solution.
The evaluation covers 13 architectures spanning MLP, tri-plane, and multi-resolution hash-table families. Processing hash-based NeRFs directly from their parameters is a useful new capability.

The rendering and contrastive objectives have complementary, empirically supported roles. The contrastive term substantially improves cross-architecture classification and instance retrieval, while the rendering objective preserves class separability.
The method generally transfers to unseen hyperparameter variants within the training architecture families and outperforms architecture-specific methods in the single-architecture setting.
The paper is clearly written and organized, with detailed architecture, optimization, dataset, and hardware information. The qualitative results complement the quantitative analysis.
weaknesses: The term “architecture-agnostic” is too strong. Every tested unseen architecture is a hyperparameter variant of one of three families observed during training; the work does not test a held-out architecture family or substantially different NeRF computation graph.

Generalization is inconsistent for more disruptive variants. Accuracy falls sharply on TRI-16W, TRI-8C, and HASH-11T in several settings, sometimes approaching poor performance even when the classifier is trained on ALL.

The experimental scope is dominated by one synthetic object-centric dataset, ShapeNetRender. The Objaverse evaluation is qualitative, uses only an already-seen MLP architecture, and lacks retrieval ground truth, so it provides limited evidence of domain generalization.

Absolute instance-retrieval performance remains modest: ALL/ALL recall@1 is only 5.3%, and cross-family recall@1 ranges from 9.5% to 33.3%. Calling these embeddings broadly effective for retrieval therefore requires qualification.

Multi-architecture experiments compare mainly against the authors’ loss variants because prior methods cannot accept mixed architectures. Useful architecture-independent alternatives—such as embeddings derived from rendered views or sampled radiance-field outputs—are missing, leaving the practical advantage of direct weight processing insufficiently quantified.

The ablations are limited: there is no study of alternative contrastive losses, loss weights, graph encodings, pooling mechanisms, or the information encoded by hash-table indices. Results also lack multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, and statistical testing.

Training takes roughly two weeks on an RTX A6000, yet the paper does not report graph sizes, memory use, inference latency, or scaling behavior. This matters because the proposed hash-table graph can contain many thousands of edges.

Overall, this is a technically solid and relevant contribution that is slightly above the acceptance threshold, but its narrow generalization study, weak retrieval accuracy, and missing baselines prevent an unqualified accept score.
